stories.title: Trump claims revised economic data shows pre-midterms figures were ‘fake’ | First Thing
stories.summary: President calls for investigation after GDP figures were adjusted upwards, despite revisions to official economic figures being commonplace. Plus, the weird and macabre world of Victorian Christmas cards Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Good morning. Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party. In a holiday message on his Truth Social platform, the US president wished a happy Thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”. Why did Trump call the figures fake? Revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, but Trump has tried repeatedly to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is under way in the US. “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”. What other acerbic well-wishes did Trump offer? He wished “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”. Why are the ballots at the center of an ongoing dispute over the 2020 election? Some Republicans, led by Trump, claimed the election results had been rigged despite Joe Biden being certified after several recounts. Republican state officials had refused to overturn the result, despite a now-infamous phone call from Trump to pressure the Georgia secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, to “find 11,780 votes”.
